reason: Refuted on three grounds, one of them a misread of the evidence itself. GROUND ONE, the page that was read is not the page that is cited. I downloaded the full text of the archive item the verdict names, archive.org/details/scotsmusicalmuse05john, and read the Auld Langsyne region. That volume is not the 1796 book of songs: it is the notes volume of the Blackwood reissue, Stenhouse's Illustrations with Laing's Additional Illustrations bound after them, and its note on CCCCXIII runs as prose commentary on pages 373 to 376 with the running head CCCCXIII. AULD LANGSYNE. The words the verifier quotes as the text under the music at song 413 are not at song 413. They are the underlay of a tune Stenhouse ANNEXES to his own note, introduced in the sentence just above it: As the latter air has, in a great measure, supplanted the proper tune of Auld Langsyne, it is here annexed. That annexed reprint is what carries the heading the verdict quotes, AULD LANGSYNE. An old Scotch drinking Song, with additions by Burns. Time, I fee'd a lad at Michaelmas. So the 1796 vol. V leaf was never opened, and with it the one thing a verse card must have: the edition's own lineation and punctuation. The underlay is syllabic, hyphenated ne-ver across the stave, and reads forgot with a point, not the comma the verdict asserts, and its stanza closes And days o' lang syne, not the familiar fourth line. The wording of lines 1 to 2 in the 1796 Museum is therefore unestablished, and lines 1 to 2 is not even a lineation on the page that was read. GROUND TWO, the byline credits Burns for the words he is least likely to have written, and the note does not say so. The note in the same volume is explicit: Burns communicated this old fragment, with the third and fourth verses written by himself, to the publisher of the Museum. Johnson accordingly marked it with the letter Z, which was usually put to old songs with additions or alterations. Cromek's report follows: He admitted to Johnson, that three of the stanzas of Langsyne only were old, the other two being written by himself. These three stanzas relate to the cup, the pint stoup, and a gude willie-waught, and the two Burns added are the ones about the braes and the burn. Stanza one, which is the whole of the shipped quotation, is on that account part of the old fragment, not part of the additions. The proposed note says only that three of the five stanzas were old and that the wording is first attested in his text; it does not say the plain thing, that the two lines being shipped are the old part. Attributed to Robert Burns is then not a hedge but a misdirection. GROUND THREE, scope, and this one is fatal on its own. The brief puts song lyrics out of scope, and puts proverbs and anonymous traditions out of scope. This is a song, printed in a song museum, under an editorial heading that calls it an old Scotch drinking Song, unsigned and marked Z for old verses with additions, with a tune named in the header. The house precedent points the other way: the one Burns already landed, in June, is from a printed book of poems, To a Louse in the Kilmarnock Poems of 1786. NO BETTER CITATION IS OFFERED, because the correct move is to drop the line rather than re-cite it. If the editor wants these words at all, the only honest form is anonymous old song, which the brief excludes; and the Museum's own note prints the ancestor, Watson's Choice Collection, Part III, Edinburgh 1711, Old Long-syne, which reads Should old Acquaintance be forgot And never thought upon, a different wording that shows how far back the formula runs. WHAT IS NOT WRONG: Robert Burns is at 1 of 3 on shipped.js, not banned, nothing shipped and no near opening, and no second Burns stands in month 8; the source line is 106 characters with no dash; the quotation ends in a question mark. Those pass. The citation, the byline and the scope do not.
